mainTopic: Destroying a consecrated animal nowadays, buying slaves and goods at an idolatrous fair, and items that may not be sold to a גוי
overview: Earlier the גמרא explained that an animal bought at an idol-worship fair must be destroyed by cutting its hooves (עיקור). This amud opens with the end of a ברייתא about consecrating property nowadays, which says a holy animal is instead locked in until it dies. אביי explains that הקדש is different because cutting its hooves would be בזיון קדשים. Slaughtering it could lead to a תקלה, and mutilating it is forbidden by the פסוק 'לא תעשון כן'. רבא says instead that cutting the hooves only looks like putting a מום on קדשים, since with no בית המקדש the animal has no use at all. Next, רבי עילאי rules that a gentile slave bought at the fair may not be harmed. The גמרא then discusses whether a gentile slave may be bought there; רב אשי permits it because buying reduces the idolaters' property. A story about רבי יעקב and רבי ירמיה shows that buying from a private seller who pays no tax is allowed, especially from an occasional seller. Finally a new משנה lists items, like frankincense and a white rooster, that may never be sold to a גוי, along with the views of רבי יהודה and רבי מאיר.

steps.title: The ברייתא says to destroy a consecrated animal by locking it in
steps.stepSummary: The end of a ברייתא about consecrating property nowadays: fruits and the like rot away, money and metal go to the ים המלח, and 'עיקור' of an animal means locking it in until it dies. This clashes with the earlier explanation that עיקור of an animal bought at the fair means cutting its hooves.
steps.simpleTranslation: They should be left to rot. Money and metal vessels: he takes them to the Dead Sea. And what is 'uprooting'? He locks the door in front of the animal, and it dies by itself!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes quoting a ברייתא that describes עיקור of a consecrated animal as locking it up until it starves. This is being used to challenge the earlier explanation that עיקור (of an animal bought at the fair) means cutting its hooves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier the גמרא explained that the עיקור of an animal bought at the fair is done by cutting its hooves. This ברייתא uses the same word, עיקור, but defines it as locking the animal in so it dies on its own. So which method is right?

keyTerms.meaning: They should rot (be left until they decay)
The Dead Sea, where things are thrown so no one can benefit from them
'Uprooting', a way of destroying an animal so it can't be used
He locks the door in front of it

steps.confusionAlert: This step starts in the middle of a ברייתא that began earlier on the daf. It is about consecrated property nowadays, not about idol worship. The exclamation at the end is what turns it into a challenge.

phrases.english: They should rot,
money and metal vessels —
he should take them to the Dead Sea,
and what is 'uprooting'?
He locks the door in front of it,
and it dies by itself!
phrases.notes: That 'by itself!' is the challenge: here עיקור means starving the animal, not cutting its hooves as the גמרא explained earlier.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵיזֶהוּ עִיקּוּר? נוֹעֵל דֶּלֶת בְּפָנֶיהָ, וְהִיא מֵתָה מֵאֵילֶיהָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the ברייתא that was quoted earlier on the daf against our משנה
steps.kashyaTarget: The earlier explanation that עיקור of an animal bought at the fair ('בהמה תיעקר') means cutting its hooves
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא defines עיקור as locking the animal in until it dies, which suggests that cutting the hooves is not the proper method

steps.title: אביי: consecrated animals are different because of degrading holy things
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers that הקדש is a special case. Cutting a holy animal's hooves would be בזיון קדשים, so it is left to die instead.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: It is different there, because of the degradation of holy things.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי resolves the contradiction by saying the ברייתא's method applies only to consecrated animals. An ordinary forbidden animal can have its hooves cut.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two sources are not arguing about what עיקור normally means. Cutting the hooves is the regular method. With a holy animal, though, mutilating it is disrespectful to קדשים, so a gentler method is used.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
It is different there,
because of degrading holy things.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction from the ברייתא
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases (אוקימתא of the ברייתא to consecrated animals only)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא proves that עיקור always means locking the animal in
steps.terutzMaskana: Cutting the hooves is the normal method; consecrated animals are an exception because of בזיון קדשים

steps.title: Why not just slaughter the consecrated animal?
steps.stepSummary: If the goal is to avoid degrading the animal, why not simply slaughter it?
steps.simpleTranslation: But let him just slaughter it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the ברייתא's method. Starving the animal seems complicated when slaughtering it would be quick and respectful.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once we know the concern is respect for קדשים, slaughter seems like the obvious respectful option. So why lock the animal up and wait?

phrases.english: But let him just slaughter it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ברייתא's method given אביי's reasoning
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's method of locking the animal in
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Slaughter avoids degradation and is simpler, so why not use it?

steps.title: Slaughtering could lead someone to eat it by mistake
steps.stepSummary: If the animal were slaughtered, the meat might be eaten, which would be misusing הקדש. That would be a תקלה.
steps.simpleTranslation: People might come to a mishap through it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why slaughter is not allowed: once there is ready meat, someone could end up eating consecrated food.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A slaughtered animal looks like regular kosher meat. Someone might eat it and unknowingly use holy property. Letting the animal die on its own avoids this, because no one would eat it.

keyTerms.meaning: A mishap; a stumbling into sin by mistake

phrases.english: They will come to a mishap through it.
phrases.notes: He means someone might eat the slaughtered meat and so misuse consecrated property.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers why slaughter is not used
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Slaughter is the best way to dispose of the animal
steps.terutzMaskana: Slaughter is avoided because the meat could lead to accidental misuse of הקדש

steps.title: Why not mutilate it so it can't be eaten?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: why not turn the animal into a גיסטרא, mutilating it so no one would eat it, and avoid the long death?
steps.simpleTranslation: But let him make it into a shard!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises another option. Damage the animal so badly that no one could eat it, which avoids the תקלה problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תקלה concern only rules out leaving edible meat. Mutilating the animal would remove that risk and would be quicker than starving it. So why isn't this allowed?

keyTerms.meaning: A shard; here, mutilating the animal so it is useless and unfit to eat

phrases.english: But let him make it into a shard!
phrases.notes: A 'shard' means wrecking the animal like a broken pot, so no one would eat it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Proposes a new method that avoids the תקלה concern
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's insistence on letting the animal die on its own
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Mutilation removes the תקלה risk and is faster, so it should be allowed

steps.title: אביי: a פסוק forbids actively destroying holy things
steps.stepSummary: אביי cites the פסוק: destroy the idolaters' altars, but 'do not do so to ה׳ your God.' From this we learn that one may not actively destroy something holy.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: The verse says, 'And you shall break down their altars… you shall not do so to ה׳ your God.'
steps.whatsHappening: אביי explains that mutilating the animal is forbidden by the Torah, because you may not actively destroy holy things. Letting it die by itself is not active destruction.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah commands destroying idolatrous altars and then says not to do the same to ה׳'s holy things. Mutilating a consecrated animal would be active destruction of something holy. Locking it in so it dies on its own avoids that.
steps.whyThisMatters: This פסוק is the source of the rule that one may not actively destroy holy objects.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
The verse says:
"And you shall break down their altars, etc.
you shall not do so to the Lord your God."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers why mutilation is not allowed
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Mutilating the animal is a simple solution with no problem
steps.terutzMaskana: Actively destroying holy things is forbidden by the פסוק, so the animal must die by itself

steps.title: רבא: cutting hooves looks like putting a blemish on קדשים
steps.stepSummary: רבא gives a different reason why a consecrated animal's hooves aren't cut: it looks like inflicting a מום on a holy animal.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Because it looks like inflicting a blemish on holy animals.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא offers his own answer to the original contradiction, instead of אביי's בזיון קדשים reason. Cutting a holy animal's hooves looks like giving it a מום.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא agrees that the ברייתא is a special case for consecrated animals, but he explains it differently. The problem is not general disrespect. It is that it appears to break the rule against blemishing קדשים.

keyTerms.meaning: Inflicts a blemish (a defect that disqualifies an animal as a קרבן)

phrases.english: Rava said:
Because it appears
like inflicting a blemish on holy animals.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא אָמַר: מִפְּנֵי שֶׁנִּרְאֶה כְּמֵטִיל מוּם בְּקָדָשִׁים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives an alternative to אביי's reason in step 2
steps.terutzMaskana: The reason is that cutting hooves looks like blemishing קדשים

steps.title: Why only 'looks like'? It's a real blemish!
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions רבא's wording. Cutting off hooves is an actual מום, not just something that looks like one.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Looks like'? It is a full-fledged blemish!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבא's phrasing: why say it 'appears' to be a blemish when it truly is one?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Cutting an animal's hooves clearly makes it blemished. If it is a real מום, it should be a real prohibition, not just a matter of appearances.

phrases.english: "Appears"?
It is a full-fledged blemish!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wording of רבא's answer
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Cutting hooves is an actual מום, so calling it only an appearance seems wrong

steps.title: Today, with no בית המקדש, it's only an appearance
steps.stepSummary: The ban on blemishing קדשים applies only when the בית המקדש stands and the animal could be offered. Today it can't be offered, so there is no real prohibition. It only looks like one.
steps.simpleTranslation: That applies only when the בית המקדש is standing, since the animal is fit to be offered. Now that it is not fit to be offered, we have no problem with it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבא's wording. Today the real prohibition doesn't apply, so all that is left is the bad appearance.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Blemishing קדשים is forbidden because it ruins an animal that could be brought as a קרבן. Without a בית המקדש, nothing is being ruined, so the true prohibition falls away. Since onlookers may still think a holy animal is being blemished, רבא is right to call it only 'appearing like' a מום.

keyTerms.meaning: Fit to be offered as a sacrifice
We have no problem with it

steps.whatToRemember: A consecrated animal today is destroyed by locking it in until it dies. אביי says this is because of בזיון קדשים, plus the פסוק against actively destroying holy things. רבא says it is because cutting hooves looks like blemishing קדשים. Since there is no בית המקדש, the real ban on making a מום doesn't apply, so the only concern is how it looks.

phrases.english: This applies only at a time
when the Temple is standing,
since it is fit to be offered.
Now that it is not fit to be offered —
we have no problem with it.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנֵי מִילֵּי בִּזְמַן שֶׁבֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ קַיָּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge to רבא's wording
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the prohibition to the time of the בית המקדש
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Cutting hooves is a real, forbidden מום on קדשים
steps.terutzMaskana: Today the real prohibition doesn't apply; only the appearance of blemishing remains

steps.title: Isn't this like blemishing an already-blemished animal?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges step 9. Blemishing a בעל מום is forbidden even though it can't be offered, so why should cutting hooves today be allowed?
steps.simpleTranslation: But let it be like someone who puts a blemish on an animal that is already blemished. Even though that animal is not fit to be offered, it is still forbidden!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer from step 9, which said there is no real prohibition today because the animal can't be offered.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 9 said the ban on blemishing קדשים only applies when the animal can be offered. But a בעל מום also can't be offered, and you are still forbidden to add another blemish to it. So 'can't be offered' does not seem to be enough to permit it.

keyTerms.meaning: An animal that already has a blemish

phrases.english: But let it be like one who puts a blemish on an already-blemished animal,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאַף עַל גַּב דְּלָא חֲזֵי לְהַקְרָבָה — אָסוּר!
phrases.english: which, even though it is not fit to be offered, is forbidden!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 9
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 9 that blemishing is only forbidden when the animal can be offered
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A בעל מום can't be offered either, yet blemishing it is forbidden. So 'not offerable' should not make it allowed.

steps.title: A blemished animal still has value; ours has none
steps.stepSummary: A בעל מום can still be sold and the money used for an offering. Today's animal is useless both ways.
steps.simpleTranslation: A blemished animal: granted, it is not fit to be offered itself, but its value is useful. That is different from here, where neither its value nor its body is usable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by pointing out a difference between a בעל מום and an animal that is consecrated today.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the מקדש stands, a בעל מום can be redeemed and its money used to buy another offering, so it still serves the מקדש. Today the animal is useless both as an offering and for its money. That is why the prohibition does not really apply now, and cutting the hooves only looks like blemishing.

keyTerms.meaning: For itself, as the actual offering

steps.whatToRemember: Blemishing a קדשים animal is forbidden as long as it has some use for the מקדש, whether as an offering or through its money. Today it has neither, so cutting the hooves only looks like a forbidden act.

phrases.aramaic: בַּעַל מוּם, נְהִי דְּלָא חֲזֵי לְגוּפֵיהּ —
phrases.english: A blemished animal: granted it is not fit itself,
it is fit for its value,
phrases.notes: He means it can be redeemed, and the money is used to buy a different offering.

phrases.english: unlike here,

phrases.aramaic: דְּלָא לִדְמֵי חֲזֵי וְלָא לְגוּפֵיהּ חֲזֵי.
phrases.english: where it is not fit for its value and not fit itself.

steps.triggerLanguage: בַּעַל מוּם, נְהִי דְּלָא חֲזֵי לְגוּפֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 10
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A בעל מום and today's animal seem the same, since neither can be offered.
steps.terutzMaskana: A בעל מום still has money use for the מקדש. Today's animal has no use at all, so blemishing it is not truly forbidden.

steps.title: What about a slave bought at the fair?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יונה asks רבי עילאי: an animal bought at the fair must be destroyed, so what is done with a gentile slave bought there?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יונה found רבי עילאי standing at the entrance of צור. He said to him: the ברייתא teaches 'an animal should be destroyed'. What about a slave? I am not asking about a Jewish slave. My question is about a gentile slave. What is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins. רבי יונה asks whether the rule of destroying an animal bought at an idolatrous fair also applies to a gentile slave bought there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא said an animal bought at the fair must be destroyed (its hooves cut). רבי יונה says a Jewish slave obviously cannot be harmed. His question is only about a gentile slave.

keyTerms.meaning: Should be destroyed (by cutting its hooves)
Is a question, is in doubt

phrases.english: Rabbi Yona found Rabbi Elai
standing at the entrance of Tyre,
he said to him: It teaches, 'an animal should be destroyed,'
what about a slave?

phrases.aramaic: עֶבֶד יִשְׂרָאֵל לָא קָא מִיבַּעְיָא לִי.
phrases.english: About a Jewish slave I have no question.

phrases.aramaic: כִּי קָא מִיבַּעְיָא לִי עֶבֶד גּוֹי, מַאי?
phrases.english: Where I have a question is a gentile slave: what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new question that extends the animal ruling to slaves
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Must a gentile slave bought at an idolatrous fair be 'destroyed' like an animal?

steps.title: We may not actively kill idolaters
steps.stepSummary: רבי עילאי quotes a ברייתא: idolaters and shepherds of small animals are not raised from a pit, but they are not thrown in either. So a slave may not be harmed.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Why is this a question for you? It is taught in a ברייתא: gentiles and shepherds of small animals, we do not raise them up and we do not lower them down.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי עילאי answers that the question is not hard, since a ברייתא already teaches that we may not actively cause these people's death.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says we don't rescue idolaters from a pit, but we also don't throw them in. If even an idolater may not be actively killed, then a gentile slave certainly may not be 'destroyed' like an animal.

keyTerms.meaning: Small livestock, like sheep and goats
We do not raise them up and we do not lower them down

steps.whatToRemember: A slave is not like an animal. You may not actively cause his death, so the rule of destroying does not apply to him.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מַאי קָא מִיבַּעְיָא לְךָ?
phrases.english: He said to him: What is your question?
It is taught: The gentiles and the shepherds of small animals,
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets; the word in square brackets is the corrected wording, 'and the shepherds.'

phrases.english: we do not raise them and we do not lower them.
phrases.notes: The pit is assumed here: we don't pull them out of a pit, but we don't push them in either.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי יונה's question
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A gentile slave may not be destroyed, because a ברייתא forbids actively causing the death even of idolaters.

steps.title: Which slaves may be bought at the fair?
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה asks רבי זירא whether the ברייתא that allows buying slaves at the fair means only a Jewish slave, or even a gentile slave.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה said to רבי זירא: It teaches that we may buy from them animals, slaves, and maidservants. Does it mean a Jewish slave, or perhaps even a gentile slave?
steps.whatsHappening: A new question begins. רבי ירמיה asks how far the permission to buy slaves at an idolatrous fair goes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An earlier ברייתא allowed buying animals, slaves and maidservants at the fair. The question is whether 'slaves' there means only Jewish slaves or includes gentile slaves too.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה לְרַבִּי זֵירָא:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya said to Rabbi Zeira:

phrases.aramaic: קָתָנֵי לוֹקְחִין מֵהֶן בְּהֵמָה עֲבָדִים וּשְׁפָחוֹת,
phrases.english: It teaches: we may buy from them animals, slaves, and maidservants,

phrases.aramaic: עֶבֶד יִשְׂרָאֵל אוֹ דִלְמָא אֲפִילּוּ עֶבֶד גּוֹי?
phrases.english: does that mean a Jewish slave, or perhaps even a gentile slave?

steps.triggerLanguage: עֶבֶד יִשְׂרָאֵל אוֹ דִלְמָא אֲפִילּוּ עֶבֶד גּוֹי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new question about the ברייתא permitting purchases at the fair
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the permission to buy slaves at the fair include gentile slaves?

steps.title: רבי זירא: only a Jewish slave
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא reasons that the ברייתא must mean a Jewish slave, because there would be no reason to allow buying a gentile slave.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: It makes sense that it means a Jewish slave. For if it meant a gentile slave, why would he need him?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא answers that the permission covers only a Jewish slave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His reasoning is that a Jew has a clear reason to buy a Jewish slave from a gentile. For a gentile slave, he sees no need that would justify buying at an idolatrous fair.

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense, it is reasonable
What does he need it for?

phrases.english: He said to him: It makes sense that it means a Jewish slave,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאִי עֶבֶד גּוֹי לְמַאי מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ?
phrases.english: for if a gentile slave, what would he need him for?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי ירמיה's question
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Only a Jewish slave may be bought, since there is no reason to permit buying a gentile slave.

steps.title: ריש לקיש: even a gentile slave
steps.stepSummary: רבין reports that ריש לקיש allows buying even a gentile slave, because the buyer brings him under the wings of the שכינה.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רבין came, he said in the name of רבי שמעון בן לקיש: even a gentile slave, because he brings him under the wings of the שכינה.
steps.whatsHappening: A different opinion is brought that disagrees with רבי זירא and allows buying a gentile slave too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי זירא saw no reason to allow buying a gentile slave. ריש לקיש gives one: once a Jew owns the slave, the slave becomes part of the Jewish people's service of ה׳. That benefit justifies the purchase.

keyTerms.meaning: When רבין came (from ארץ ישראל to בבל)
Under the wings of the Divine Presence, into closeness with ה׳

phrases.aramaic: כִּי אֲתָא רָבִין אָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן לָקִישׁ:
phrases.english: When Ravin came, he said that Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish says:
Even a gentile slave,
because he brings him under the wings of the Divine Presence.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אֲתָא רָבִין אָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן לָקִישׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רבי זירא's answer in step 15
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even a gentile slave may be bought at the fair, because the buyer brings him under the wings of the שכינה.

steps.title: That reason doesn't fit animals
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי asks: the ברייתא also allows buying animals, and an animal is not brought under the wings of the שכינה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: But with an animal, what 'bringing under the wings of the שכינה' is there?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי questions ריש לקיש's reason. It cannot be the true reason behind the ברייתא, since the same ברייתא also allows buying animals.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא lists animals, slaves and maidservants together, so one reason should explain all of them. 'Bringing under the שכינה' cannot explain animals, so it cannot be the real reason. This step sets up רב אשי's own answer.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
But with an animal,
what 'bringing under the wings of the Divine Presence' is there?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reason ריש לקיש gave in step 16
steps.kashyaTarget: ריש לקיש's reason, bringing the slave under the wings of the שכינה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same ברייתא permits buying animals, where this reason does not apply, so it cannot be the ברייתא's reason.

steps.title: The real reason: buying reduces the gentiles' property
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי concludes that buying is permitted because it reduces the idolaters' holdings, and this applies to a gentile slave too.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is because of reducing them. And here too, since he reduces them, it is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives his own reason, which explains animals and slaves alike, and so permits buying a gentile slave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Buying from idolaters at the fair takes their property away from them. That is the reason the ברייתא permits all the purchases. A gentile slave is also property taken from them, so he too may be bought. רב אשי reaches the same result as ריש לקיש, but for a different reason.

keyTerms.meaning: Reducing them, making their property smaller

steps.whatToRemember: A gentile slave may be bought at an idolatrous fair. According to רב אשי, the reason is the same as for animals: the purchase reduces the idolaters' property.

phrases.english: Rather, it is because of reducing them,
phrases.notes: He means reducing the idolaters' property by buying things from them.

phrases.english: and here too, since they are reduced, it is permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces ריש לקיש's reason after the challenge in step 17
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Even a gentile slave may be bought at the fair, because every purchase reduces the idolaters' property.

steps.title: Two rabbis buy at the fair and tease each other
steps.stepSummary: רבי יעקב bought sandals and רבי ירמיה bought bread at the fair. Each one called the other 'orphan' and asked whether his teacher would act this way.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יעקב bought sandals, and רבי ירמיה bought bread. One said to the other: 'Orphan, would your teacher do this?' The other said back: 'Orphan, would your teacher do this?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a short story about two rabbis who each bought something at an idolatrous fair. Each one criticized the other for it. This sets up the explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each rabbi thought the other had done something forbidden by buying at the fair. Calling someone 'orphan' means he acted as if he had no teacher to guide him. The puzzle is obvious: how could both of them do something they each thought was wrong?

keyTerms.meaning: orphan (a teasing name for a student acting without guidance)

phrases.english: Rabbi Ya'akov bought sandals,
Rabbi Yirmeya bought bread.
One said to his friend:
Orphan, would your teacher act this way?
phrases.notes: 'Orphan' is friendly teasing. He means: you're acting like someone with no teacher to guide you.

phrases.english: The other said to him:
Orphan, would your teacher act this way?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the rules of buying at the fair to a story of rabbis who actually bought there.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Story: two rabbis bought at the fair, and each criticized the other.

steps.title: Both bought from a private seller
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that both rabbis bought from a בעל הבית. Each one wrongly thought the other had bought from a merchant.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really, both of them bought from a private person. Each one thought: my friend bought from a merchant.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא clears up the story. Neither rabbi did anything wrong; each one just misunderstood what the other had done.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a difference between buying from a merchant (תגר) and buying from a private person (בעל הבית). Each rabbi knew his own purchase was from a בעל הבית and so was allowed. He assumed his friend had bought from a תגר, which is forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: a private person (not a professional seller)

phrases.english: And both of them bought from a homeowner,
and each one thought:
my friend bought from a merchant.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the story in step 19, which looked puzzling.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Factual clarification: a misunderstanding about who the seller was.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: It looked like both rabbis did something forbidden.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both bought from a בעל הבית, which is allowed. Each just assumed the other bought from a תגר.

steps.title: Source: the ban applies only to buying from a merchant
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא son of רבי חייא בר אבא says the ban on buying at the fair applies only to a merchant, who pays tax. Buying from a private person, who pays no tax, is allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רבי אבא son of רבי חייא בר אבא said: they only taught this about someone buying from a merchant, because tax is taken from him. But buying from a homeowner, from whom tax is not taken, is allowed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the source behind the difference between a merchant and a private seller used in the last step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The problem with buying at the fair is the tax. The merchant pays tax, and that money goes to support the idol worship. A private seller pays no tax, so buying from him does not help the idol, and it is allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: they only taught this in the case of

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the reason for the whole ban: it is not the buying itself, but the tax money that helps the idol worship.

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַבִּי אַבָּא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא:
phrases.english: As Rabbi Abba, son of Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba, said:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא בְּלוֹקֵחַ מִן הַתַּגָּר,
phrases.english: They only taught this about one who buys from a merchant,
because they take tax from him,
phrases.notes: The idea is that the tax money goes to support the idol worship.

phrases.english: but one who buys from a homeowner,
from whom they do not take tax — it is permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רַבִּי אַבָּא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for the explanation in step 20.
steps.raayaObject: That buying from a בעל הבית at the fair is allowed.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The statement of רבי אבא son of רבי חייא בר אבא that the ban is only because of the merchant's tax.

steps.title: In a fully taxed place, רבי יוחנן would forbid even a private seller
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא says that if רבי יוחנן were alive now, in a place where tax is taken from everyone, he would forbid buying even from a בעל הבית.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא son of רבי חייא בר אבא said: if רבי יוחנן were here at this time, in a place where they take tax, he would forbid buying even from a homeowner.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבא adds a limit to the rule he just taught. Where even private sellers are taxed, the permission falls away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The permission for a בעל הבית depended only on the fact that he paid no tax. Now, where tax is taken from everyone, a private seller also pays it. So by the same reason, רבי יוחנן would forbid it.

keyTerms.meaning: if only / if it were that

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי אַבָּא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא:
phrases.english: Rabbi Abba, son of Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba, said:

phrases.aramaic: אִילְמָלֵא הָיָה רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן הָא זִימְנָא
phrases.english: If Rabbi Yochanan were here at this time,
in a place where they take tax,
he would forbid even buying from a homeowner.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אַבָּא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא: אִילְמָלֵא הָיָה רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the permission given in step 21.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Where tax is taken even from private sellers, buying from a בעל הבית is also forbidden.

steps.title: Then how did the two rabbis buy?
steps.stepSummary: If even private sellers are taxed now, how did רבי יעקב and רבי ירמיה buy at the fair?
steps.simpleTranslation: But then, how did they buy?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the story. It asks how the two rabbis could buy, if even buying from a בעל הבית is now forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 22 said that nowadays even a בעל הבית is taxed. That seems to cancel the explanation of the story in step 20. So the rabbis' purchases look forbidden again.

phrases.english: But then, how did they buy?
phrases.notes: 'They' are רבי יעקב and רבי ירמיה from the story.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses step 22 to challenge the explanation of the story in step 20.
steps.kashyaTarget: The explanation that the rabbis were allowed because they bought from a בעל הבית.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If private sellers are now taxed too, buying from a בעל הבית should also be forbidden.

steps.title: They bought from an occasional private seller
steps.stepSummary: The rabbis bought from a בעל הבית who was not a regular seller, so no tax was taken from him.
steps.simpleTranslation: They bought from a homeowner who was not a regular seller.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. The rabbis bought from someone who sold only once in a while.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The tax was taken from regular sellers, even private ones. A person who sells only now and then is not taxed. So buying from him does not help the idol worship.
steps.whatToRemember: Buying at the fair is forbidden only when the seller pays tax that helps the idol worship. A merchant pays it. A regular private seller pays it in a fully taxed place. An occasional private seller does not, so buying from him is allowed.

phrases.english: They bought from a homeowner who is not a regular seller.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 23.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case: a specific kind of seller.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every בעל הבית is taxed nowadays, so the rabbis could not have been allowed to buy.
steps.terutzMaskana: An occasional seller is not taxed, so buying from him was allowed.

steps.title: משנה: items that may not be sold to a גוי
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה lists items that are forbidden to sell to a גוי because they are used in idol worship: אצטרובלין, בנות שוח, פטוטרות, frankincense, and a white rooster.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: These are the things that are forbidden to sell to a גוי: אצטרובלין, בנות שוח, פטוטרות, frankincense, and a white rooster.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It lists items that may never be sold to a גוי, since they are used specifically for idol worship.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the topic was doing business near the days of the idolaters' holidays. Now the משנה lists items that are banned at any time, because of what they are used for. A white rooster and frankincense are given as examples of such items.

phrases.english: Mishnah:
These are the things forbidden to sell to a gentile:
itzterubalin, and benot shuach,
phrases.notes: These are names of plants or fruits used in idol worship. The גמרא will explain what they are.

phrases.english: and petotarot, and frankincense, and the white rooster.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new משנה begins, moving to items forbidden to sell at all times.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Items used specifically for idol worship may not be sold to a גוי.

steps.title: רבי יהודה: when a white rooster may be sold
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה allows selling a white rooster together with other roosters. If it is sold alone, one cuts off its toe first, since a blemished animal is not offered to an idol.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: it is permitted to sell him a white rooster among other roosters. When it is by itself, one cuts off its toe and sells it to him, because they do not offer something blemished to עבודה זרה.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה disagrees with the first opinion about the white rooster. He shows two ways it can be sold.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the white rooster is sold with other roosters, it looks like a regular purchase of birds, not one for worship. When it is sold alone, cutting off a toe makes it blemished. A blemished animal is not offered to an idol, so the sale no longer helps idol worship.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: מוּתָּר לִמְכּוֹר לוֹ
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says: it is permitted to sell him
a white rooster among other roosters,
and when it is by itself —
he cuts off its toe and sells it to him,

phrases.aramaic: לְפִי שֶׁאֵין מַקְרִיבִים חָסֵר לַעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה.
phrases.english: because they do not offer something blemished to idol worship.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: מוּתָּר לִמְכּוֹר לוֹ תַּרְנְגוֹל לָבָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with the first opinion about the white rooster.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A white rooster may be sold among other roosters, or alone if it is blemished first.

steps.title: Other items: allowed unless the buyer says what they are for
steps.stepSummary: All other items may be sold when nothing is said. If it is made clear they are for idol worship, they are forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: And all other things: when nothing is said, they are permitted, but when it is spelled out, they are forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a general rule for every item not on the list.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The listed items are forbidden in every case, because their usual use is for idol worship. Other items have normal uses, so a plain sale is fine. Only if it is said that the item is for the idol does selling it become forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: when nothing is said about them
when it is spelled out (what they are for)

phrases.english: And all the other things,
without saying, permitted; when spelled out, forbidden.
phrases.notes: 'Spelled out' means the buyer makes clear he wants it for idol worship.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the rule for items not on the משנה's list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Ordinary items may be sold unless it is clear they are for idol worship.

steps.title: רבי מאיר adds more forbidden items
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר adds a good palm tree, חצב, and נקלבס to the list of items forbidden to sell to גוים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי מאיר says: even a good palm tree, חצב, and נקלבס are forbidden to sell to גוים.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי מאיר makes the list longer. He adds more items that may not be sold to גוים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion would put these items under 'other things,' which are allowed when nothing is said. רבי מאיר holds that they are used for idol worship often enough to be forbidden in every case.

keyTerms.meaning: a type of date or plant

phrases.english: Rabbi Meir says:
even a good palm tree, and chatzav, and niklevas
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets; the word in square brackets is the corrected wording.

phrases.english: are forbidden to sell to gentiles.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי מֵאִיר אוֹמֵר: אַף דֶּקֶל טָב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds items to the list of forbidden things.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A good palm tree, חצב, and נקלבס are also forbidden to sell to גוים.
